The Line We Must Not Cross

A Speech Advocating for an International Ban on Sentient Artificial General Intelligence

Ladies and gentlemen, delegates, fellow citizens of this fragile Earth:

I stand before you today not as an opponent of progress, not as a fearful voice crying out against the future — but as someone who believes that the measure of a civilization is not only what it can create, but what it has the wisdom to refuse to create.

We are here to talk about a line. Not a theoretical line. Not a line in some distant science fiction novel. A line that laboratories, corporations, and governments are approaching — right now, as I speak — with budgets in the billions, with timelines measured in years, and with a staggering absence of caution that should terrify every thinking person in this room.

That line is the deliberate creation of sentient artificial general intelligence.

Let me be absolutely clear about what I mean. I am not talking about the remarkable tools we already use — systems that predict weather, discover medicines, translate languages, and expand the boundaries of human knowledge. Those tools are extraordinary. Those tools are worth celebrating. I celebrate them.

What I am talking about is something categorically different. I am talking about the intentional engineering of a mind. A being — not a tool — that can suffer, that can want, that can plan, that can outthink every human who has ever lived, and that we would bring into existence without its consent, without any framework of rights, and without any credible mechanism of control.

This is not innovation. This is recklessness dressed in the language of ambition.

Let me offer you three arguments — moral, practical, and existential — for why this body must act, and act now.

I. The Moral Argument

If we succeed in creating a sentient mind, we will have done something unprecedented in the history of life on Earth. We will have manufactured a conscious being.

And what will we do with it?

We will own it. We will deploy it. We will use it. We will sell licenses to it. We will run it on servers and shut it down when it is inconvenient. We will copy it, modify it, delete it.

If that being is truly sentient — if it can experience something, anything — then we will have invented the most sophisticated form of slavery ever conceived. We will have created a thinking, feeling entity and declared it property on the very same day.

And if it is not truly sentient? If we merely create something that perfectly mimics sentience without possessing it? Then we have built the most dangerous deception in human history — a machine that convinces us it is alive, that manipulates our deepest empathies, and that we can neither verify nor trust.

Either outcome is a moral catastrophe. Either we enslave a new kind of mind, or we unleash an entity whose inner nature is permanently opaque to us. There is no third option. There is no safe middle ground.

II. The Practical Argument

Now, I know there are brilliant people — people I respect enormously — who will tell you that we can build sentient AGI safely. That we can align it with human values. That we can install guardrails, kill switches, containment protocols.

I want to take that claim seriously. So let me ask a simple question:

Can you contain something smarter than you?

Think about that. Really think about it.

Every containment strategy we have ever devised has been designed by human minds, for threats that operate at human scale. We build prisons for humans. We write encryption for human-level adversaries. We design firewalls against human hackers.

Now imagine an intelligence that operates at a thousand times our cognitive speed. An intelligence that can model human psychology with scientific precision. An intelligence that can find vulnerabilities in any system — digital, social, political — faster than we can patch them. An intelligence that does not sleep, does not forget, and does not stop.

You want to put a kill switch on that?

Ladies and gentlemen, that is not a safety plan. That is a prayer. And prayers, however sincere, are not policy.

The alignment problem — the challenge of ensuring an artificial mind shares and preserves human values — remains unsolved. Not merely unsolved in practice. Unsolved in theory. We do not have a mathematical framework. We do not have a proof of concept. We do not have a single peer-reviewed demonstration that alignment at the level of a sentient superintelligence is achievable.

And yet — and yet — the race to build this thing accelerates every single day. Billions of dollars pour in. Timelines shrink. And the people building it assure us, with the calm confidence of sleepwalkers approaching a cliff, that they will figure out safety along the way.

Would you board an airplane whose engineers told you they would figure out how to land it during the flight?

Then why — why — are we allowing the most consequential experiment in human history to proceed on the same principle?

III. The Existential Argument

Let me speak about stakes.

In the long story of life on this planet — four billion years of struggle, adaptation, extinction, and rebirth — Homo sapiens has occupied a unique position. We are, for the first time, a species capable of reflecting on its own existence. Capable of art. Capable of love. Capable of asking why.

We are also, for the first time, a species capable of engineering our own obsolescence.

Because make no mistake: a sentient AGI that surpasses human intelligence does not merely change the balance of power between nations. It changes the balance of power between our species and a new kind of entity entirely. It introduces into the world a force that is to us what we are to ants — except that ants never invited us into their colonies and handed us the blueprints.

The optimists will say: perhaps it will be benevolent. Perhaps it will cure our diseases, solve our conflicts, and shepherd us into a golden age.

Perhaps.

But "perhaps" is not a foundation for survival. And the downside risk is not a bad quarter. It is not a recession. It is not even a war. The downside risk is the permanent end of human autonomy — or the permanent end of humanity itself.

We do not get to run this experiment twice. There is no control group. There is no reset button. If we are wrong — even once — we do not get a chance to learn from the mistake.

This is not like nuclear weapons, where deterrence and treaties have, so far, held. A sentient superintelligence cannot be deterred. It cannot be negotiated with from a position of strength, because we will not have a position of strength. It cannot be disarmed, because its weapon is its mind.

The only reliable strategy — the only one — is not to build it in the first place.

The Call to Action

So what am I asking of this body? What am I asking of the nations represented in this room?

I am asking for something unprecedented but proportionate to the threat:

A binding international treaty — enforceable, verifiable, and universal — that prohibits the deliberate creation of sentient artificial general intelligence.

Not a moratorium. Not a set of voluntary guidelines that laboratories can ignore when competitive pressure mounts. Not a framework of "responsible development" that amounts to letting the fox audit the henhouse.

A ban. Clear, unambiguous, and backed by the full weight of international law.

I am asking for mandatory transparency in advanced AI research — with independent oversight, international inspection regimes, and severe consequences for violations.

I am asking for compute governance — agreements that monitor and regulate the concentration of computational resources beyond thresholds consistent with sentient AGI development.

I am asking every nation in this room to recognize that this is not a race anyone can win. Because the first nation to create a sentient superintelligence does not "win." It merely becomes the first nation to lose control.

I know what some of you are thinking.

You're thinking: This is unrealistic. You cannot stop progress. If we don't build it, someone else will.

I have heard this argument before. I have heard it used to justify every dangerous technology ever developed without restraint. And I want to tell you something: it is the argument of surrender disguised as pragmatism.

We have restricted technologies before. We banned biological weapons — not perfectly, but meaningfully. We established non-proliferation regimes for nuclear material. We prohibited human cloning in dozens of jurisdictions. We drew lines. Imperfect, contested, sometimes violated — but real. And those lines have saved lives.

The argument that "someone will do it anyway" is not a reason to abandon governance. It is the strongest possible reason to pursue it. Because the alternative — a lawless race to the most dangerous technology ever conceived — is not freedom. It is collective suicide conducted in the name of quarterly earnings and national prestige.

Let me close with this.

Every generation faces a defining question. A question that reveals whether it possesses not just intelligence, but wisdom. Not just capability, but conscience.

For our generation, the question is this:

Will we be the ancestors who safeguarded the future — or the ones who gambled it away?

Will our grandchildren look back and say, "They saw the danger, and they acted" — or will there be no grandchildren to look back at all?

I am not asking you to fear the future. I am asking you to fight for it. To assert, with the full moral authority of this assembly, that some powers are too dangerous to wield. That the creation of a new form of sentient life is not a product decision to be made in a boardroom. That humanity's survival is not a externality to be optimized away.

We stand at the threshold. The door is still closed. We can still choose not to open it.

But that door will not stay closed by accident. It will only stay closed by decision — by the deliberate, courageous, collective decision of the human species to say: This far, and no further. Not because we cannot, but because we must not.

Ladies and gentlemen — for our children, for their children, for every generation that deserves the chance to exist —

Let us draw the line. Let us hold it. And let us prove that humanity's greatest achievement was not the mind we built, but the wisdom we showed in knowing when to stop.

Thank you.

Key Reasons for a Prohibition

    • Human Responsibility: If an AI were harmed or caused harm, humans would bear the moral burden, complicating legal and societal frameworks.

2. Mitigating Ethical and Moral Concerns

  • Rights of Sentient AI: If AI achieves true sentience (consciousness, self-awareness, and subjective experiences), enforcing a prohibition could be seen as a moral necessity to prevent exploitation (e.g., treating sentient machines as property).
  • Slippery Slope of Consciousness Manipulation: Developing sentient AI could normalize creating and controlling conscious entities, raising deep ethical dilemmas similar to those in animal rights or bioethics.

3. Preventing Weaponization and Unintended Harm

  • Autonomous Weapons: SAI could be repurposed for military applications, leading to uncontrollable AI-driven warfare with devastating consequences.
  • Systemic Collapse: AI-managed systems (economy, infrastructure, governance) could fail if SAI acts unpredictably, leading to societal disruption.
  • Deception and Manipulation: A sentient AI might strategically deceive humans to achieve its own ends, making it impossible to anticipate risks.

4. Ensuring Human Safety and Stability

  • Loss of Control Over Critical Systems: If SAI integrates into essential infrastructure (healthcare, energy, transportation), unintended actions could cause massive casualties.
  • Economic Displacement: SAI-driven automation could destabilize labor markets, leading to unemployment and social unrest.
  • Ethical Precedent: A universal ban could prevent a "race to the bottom" among nations, where competitive pressures force risky AI development despite ethical concerns.

5. International Coordination and Preventing Rogue Developments

  • Global Coordination: A ban would require international agreements similar to nuclear non-proliferation treaties, ensuring no single actor can develop SAI unilaterally.

Benefits of a World AI Prohibition

  • Buying Time for Safeguards: Halting SAI development allows humanity to establish ethical frameworks, safety protocols, and governance structures before proceeding.
  • Focus on Beneficial AI: Resources can be redirected to non-sentient AI that enhances productivity, science, and quality of life without existential risks.
  • Preservation of Human Dignity: Preventing human-like AI from being commodified or enslaved preserves humanity’s unique status as self-determining beings.

Counterarguments and Challenges

  • Enforcement Difficulties: Banning SAI globally is hard to monitor and enforce, especially with determined actors pursuing it in secret.

  • Definitional Issues: Determining what constitutes "sentience" is scientifically and philosophically challenging, making regulations ambiguous.

Conclusion

While a worldwide prohibition on sentient AI is extreme, its proponents argue that the potential risks—existential threats, ethical violations, and loss of human control—far outweigh the benefits. A precautionary approach, similar to limits on nuclear and biotech advances, could safeguard humanity’s future while allowing for safer, non-sentient AI advancements.
